title: New Route, Old Networks: The Lobito Corridor Dilemma
summary: Maya and Daniel break down a November 2026 policy brief from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime on the Lobito Corridor. They explore how billions in Western infrastructure investment aimed at securing critical minerals risk entrenching existing criminal economies across Central Africa.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome to the podcast. Today we are unpacking a really crucial policy brief just published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is titled 'New Route, Old Networks: Organized crime along the Lobito Corridor', written by Nathalia Dukhan and Zobel Behalal. And if you follow critical minerals, Western supply chain policy, or Central African security, this is something you definitely need to pay attention to.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, because the Lobito Corridor has basically been billed as the flagship Western infrastructure play in Africa. We are talking about connecting the rich copper and cobalt deposits of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia straight across Angola to the Atlantic port of Lobito. The European Union has mobilized two billion euros. Washington and other backers have pledged more than six billion dollars in total. It is supposed to be the clean, direct democratic alternative to Chinese-dominated supply routes.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. On paper, it is transformative. Cutting transport times from roughly twenty-five days by road down to Durban in South Africa to just eight days by rail to the Atlantic. In fact, the first shipment of Congolese copper concentrate hit Lobito back in December 2023, and refined copper anodes from Kamoa-Kakula followed in April 2026. But the core thesis of this GI-TOC brief is that a railway line is not built in a vacuum. It cuts straight through one of the mining regions most exposed to transnational organized crime, systemic corruption, and elite capture.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the authors make this sharp point right up front: if you do not build integrity into the system right now, while the DRC and Zambian sections are still being financed and built, you are not actually cleaning up the supply chain. You are simply building a faster, Western-funded conveyor belt for stolen, illicit, and conflict-tainted minerals.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is the paradox at the heart of the brief. The corridor is designed to reduce dependence on opaque supply chains, yet it risks becoming an integral part of them. And the brief walks through the entire pipeline, from the mine pit upstream, across the roads and borders, all the way to geopolitical sabotage and diluted Western standards.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us start upstream at the mines, because that is where the numbers in this report really jump off the page. When people think about mining violence in the DRC, they usually think of rebel groups in the eastern provinces. But in the southern Copperbelt—specifically Lualaba and Haut-Katanga—the report points out that the primary threat is not insurgencies. It is elite capture and the very state forces meant to protect the concessions.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. In Lualaba and Haut-Katanga, illegal extraction on industrial concessions has become a quasi-industrial operation generating an estimated two billion dollars a year. That is not petty scavenging. It is heavily organized, and local sources allege it is actively shielded by members of the security forces, provincial authorities, and political elites. Productive artisanal sites in Lubumbashi have been forcibly cleared of regular diggers and handed over to politically connected figures operating under armed protection.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the report highlights some striking fieldwork data on this. In 2025, the International Peace Information Service, together with the local group IBGDH and the government's own artisanal mining agency, mapped 51 artisanal mining sites in Lualaba. They found the Congolese national army present on 64 percent of them. Soldiers were not there maintaining civic peace—they were imposing illegal taxes, seizing mineral output, monopolizing goods sold to miners, and in some cases even pre-financing illegal extraction themselves.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And it comes at a terrible human cost. Roughly 200,000 artisanal miners work copper and cobalt deposits in the DRC, alongside an estimated 40,000 children. Most work outside any legal framework in hand-dug tunnels prone to catastrophic collapses. The brief mentions the tragedy at the Kalando mine in November 2025: gunfire from soldiers triggered a panic among diggers, a makeshift bridge collapsed, and at least 32 people were killed.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And when the military clears a site, it does not solve the problem. Look at what happened at Tenke Fungurume back in 2019, one of the world's largest copper-cobalt concessions. The army evicted 10,000 artisanal miners, but soldiers reportedly stayed behind to extort entry fees and run illegal extraction for senior military officers. Fast forward to July 2023, about 120 tonnes of copper cathodes disappeared from Tenke Fungurume, leading to the arrest of the regional military commander, General Smith Gihanga.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Then you have this emerging trend of outsourcing security to private military contractors. Kinshasa has contracted Erik Prince, the founder of Blackwater. While his teams deployed drone surveillance alongside government forces fighting M23 in the east, Prince also signed a five-year contract in December 2024 to improve tax collection in the mining sector. His personnel are now operating around Kolwezi, right at the starting hub of the Lobito Corridor.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which the UN Working Group on the use of mercenaries has warned about for years. When private armed actors are paid out of the mineral revenues they help secure, the line between legitimate state tax collection and armed resource extraction essentially vanishes. There is no independent oversight.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And upstream risks extend beyond copper and cobalt in the DRC. Look at Zambia's manganese sector. Zambian manganese production doubled between 2023 and 2024. But a US-funded study cited in the report found that nearly half of the workers surveyed were in forced labor, with unlicensed operations fronted by Zambian nominees for foreign investors. Because processing mills mix ores from multiple suppliers, the mineral cannot be traced back to the mine. And manganese has already begun moving along the Lobito route.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So once illicit ore leaves the pit and enters the processing circuit, it is practically laundered into the legal supply chain. But what happens during transit? The corridor aims to replace road transport with rail, but right now, most minerals still move by truck through Zambia to ports like Durban or Dar es Salaam. What is happening on those highways?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Complete predation. It reads like organized banditry with high-level institutional complicity. Between Kolwezi and the border post at Kasumbalesa, truckers face between ten and sixteen checkpoints manned by police, soldiers, and tax inspectors, shelling out between 300 and 1,200 dollars in bribes per trip. In July 2025 near Tumbwe, armed men with military radios and unmarked vehicles hijacked copper convoys carrying loads worth around six million dollars each. The report notes that police allegedly offered to 'recover' stolen trucks for 50,000 dollars and the cargo for a 10 percent fee—roughly 600,000 dollars.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Truck drivers are paying with their lives, too. In early 2026, several Zambian drivers were attacked, killed, or went missing in the DRC, leading Zambian unions to temporarily suspend cross-border trips. And this is happening on both sides of the border. In July 2026, Zambian authorities charged a former Copperbelt provincial police commissioner, a magistrate, police officers, and a court clerk over the theft and auctioning of 436 recovered copper cathodes at the Mokambo border.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Then you reach the border posts themselves, which the brief describes as the points where illicit cargo magically becomes legal. Smuggling bulk metals like copper and cobalt does not require hiding bags under floorboards; it is done through misdeclaring weight, grade, or origin. The Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative has documented pervasive misreporting at DRC border posts. Researchers cited in the brief estimate that between 2000 and 2024, anywhere from 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes of undeclared uranium left the DRC hidden inside cobalt hydroxide exports.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is an astonishing figure. 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes of undeclared uranium. And stolen copper moves through identical customs fraud. In June 2026, South African police and INTERPOL intercepted 121 tonnes of copper stolen in Zambia at City Deep in Johannesburg. It had passed through Zimbabwe via the Beitbridge border post using forged customs manifests, cloned license plates, and filed-off serial numbers.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And the fear is that the Lobito Corridor simply shifts this vulnerability to the Dilolo-Luau crossing between the DRC and Angola. While rail offers fewer transit nodes than roads, customs harmonization and data sharing between Kinshasa and Luanda have been exceedingly slow. If border processing is accelerated without upgrading automated inspection and verification, illicit cargo slips through faster than ever.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Now, let us zoom out to the geopolitical backdrop, because the international politics surrounding this corridor have shifted dramatically since it was first conceived. Tell us about that transition.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Originally, in late 2023, Lobito was framed under the EU's Global Gateway and the US Partnership for Global Infrastructure as a broad development corridor—sustainable agriculture, clean energy, local value addition, and battery manufacturing for the green transition. But by late 2025 and 2026, that framing shifted decisively toward raw supply security.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen introduced RESourceEU in late 2025 to secure access to critical raw materials against foreign weaponization. In the US, the Trump administration slashed USAID development programs along the corridor while aggressive bilateral deals took center stage. Take the US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement signed in December 2025. It gives US firms a right of first offer on strategic assets and sets targets to route half of Congo's copper and a third of its cobalt through Lobito within five years.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And look at who stepped in. The first major deal under that pact was Virtus Minerals acquiring Chemaf's copper-cobalt assets in Kolwezi and Lubumbashi. Reuters reported that Virtus executives came from security and intelligence backgrounds and had overstated their mining operational experience. Meanwhile, Kinshasa reportedly floated the Rubaya coltan site in North Kivu as a priority asset—even though it is held by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group! Kinshasa is essentially seeking US security backing in exchange for mineral access.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Zambia took a very different path, though. In May 2026, Lusaka flatly rejected US proposals that would have tied two billion dollars in five-year health aid to preferential critical mineral access for US companies. President Hichilema held out until Washington agreed to decouple the health funding from the mineral negotiations in October 2026.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Which brings us to the competition with China. China already controls stakes in 15 of the DRC's largest copper-cobalt mines and dominates global refining. In late 2025, Beijing countered Lobito by signing a 1.4-billion-dollar deal to revamp TAZARA, the railway linking Zambia to the port of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. So you have two rival corridors competing for the exact same ore.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the brief includes this fascinating section on what it terms 'geocriminality'—foreign state actors using criminal influence operations to disrupt the Lobito Corridor. Can you walk through the findings on Russian covert campaigns?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes. Drawing on investigative consortium reports from Forbidden Stories and Africa Politology—which was Wagner's influence apparatus before Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, the SVR, took direct control in late 2023—the brief outlines an aggressive hybrid campaign targeting Angola, the DRC, Namibia, and South Africa. Confidential Russian documents reveal four distinct lines of attack: first, circulating forged letters, like a fake memorandum from DRC state miner Gécamines claiming it refused to use Lobito due to exorbitant tariffs; second, fabricating claims that the Lobito concessionaire was sabotaging passenger trains to spark fatal collisions; third, stoking fears that Western loans would trap Angola in a sovereign debt crisis; and fourth, stirring resentment among Angolan state rail workers.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: While serving Beijing's commercial interest in boosting TAZARA over Lobito, even without direct operational coordination. But what really strikes me in the report is how Western regulatory standards are quietly retreating in the face of this competition. At the exact moment they should be tightening oversight, policymakers in Washington and Brussels are loosening it.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. The report calls it 'the race for volume versus standards'. In the US, there are legislative efforts in Congress to repeal Section 1502 of the Dodd-Frank Act, the bedrock of conflict minerals disclosures. In Europe, member states passed a competitiveness simplification package in February 2026 that exempts all but the largest companies from corporate due diligence and pushes mandatory compliance back to 2029. Due diligence obligations under the EU Batteries Regulation have already been kicked down the road to August 2027. And copper and cobalt are still entirely absent from the EU's 2017 Conflict Minerals Regulation.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So both sides of the Atlantic are essentially saying: secure the volume first, worry about traceability later. Which creates an enormous opening for criminal networks to capture the profits while the sovereign hosts bear the debt. Angola rebuilt its Benguela rail line heavily on Chinese credit and its debt is nearing its legal ceiling; Zambia is borrowing heavily to fund its 830-kilometer rail link to Chingola, which will not even be finished until around 2030.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Which leads directly into the policy recommendations Dukhan and Behalal lay out. They argue that because much of the corridor is still being built and financed, there is still a window of leverage.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What are the key interventions they recommend?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: First, tackle organized crime at the source. Clear the armed forces off artisanal sites, dismantle unauthorized checkpoints, and enforce clear, independent oversight of private security contractors. If a private security outfit or contractor has a history of human rights violations or economic crimes, exclude them.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Second, establish a dedicated cross-border investigative unit. Angola, the DRC, and Zambia need vetted police, customs officers, and military prosecutors working with SARPCCO and INTERPOL's regional bureau in Harare to pursue organized smuggling networks across borders, backed by independent, ring-fenced funding.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Third, turn rail terminals into mandatory traceability checkpoints. Because rail has far fewer loading points than thousands of dispersed road trucks, mine-of-origin, weight, and assay data can be digitally recorded and shared across borders. Importing countries must reconcile their customs intake with origin data to catch discrepancies immediately.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And fourth, use the financial window. Since financing for the DRC rail rehabilitation—awarded to Mota-Engil Africa in August 2026—is not yet finalized, and Zambia's AfDB-backed link is only partially funded, international lenders should tie capital tranches directly to measurable anti-corruption milestones, public contract disclosure, and anti-money laundering assessments.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Finally, the US and the EU have to hold their own deals to the standards they preach. If the EU engages in joint purchasing and stockpiling under RESourceEU, or if the US backs deals via the Development Finance Corporation, public money must never support unverified supply chains. Due diligence rules must cover copper and cobalt, not just gold and the 3Ts.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So what is the bottom line as we look ahead?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The bottom line is that modern infrastructure cannot fix governance deficits on its own. If Western partners prioritize speed over scrutiny in an effort to counter China, the Lobito Corridor will simply accelerate the extraction of illicit wealth, leaving producer nations deeper in debt and Western supply chains exposed to severe legal and reputational risks. The tracks are laid, but governance will decide what actually runs on them.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A vital reality check on one of the most celebrated infrastructure projects of the decade. That is all for this episode. You can read the full report, 'New Route, Old Networks', on the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime website.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Thanks for listening, and until next time.
